# LeakSanitizer suppressions — third-party allocations that outlive the process on purpose.
#
# A line here is a CLAIM, so each one says WHOSE allocation it is and why nobody frees it. Our own
# leaks never belong in this file: one of ours is either released by whoever created it, or it is
# explained in the code that makes it — a suppression would hide the question instead of answering
# it. (The picture auto-loader is the worked example: its destructor was empty, and the answer was
# to take down the wx image handlers it had put up, not to list them here.)
#
# Measured on the first full sanitised run, 2026-09-22: every test process reported the same
# ~31.7 KB in ~728 allocations at exit, and the largest single entry — 14848 bytes in 58 objects —
# is fontconfig's. Under a GUI application GTK is never torn down either; the difference is that a
# test binary exits while LeakSanitizer is watching.

# fontconfig keeps its font set and pattern caches in process-wide statics with no teardown that
# anyone calls; the handles die with the process by design.
leak:libfontconfig

# The GLib type system, GObject classes and the GTK singletons built from them are created once and
# deliberately never freed — g_type_init's tables have no matching shutdown.
leak:libglib
leak:libgobject
leak:libgio
leak:libgtk

# Font faces and shaping buffers held by the caches above.
leak:libfreetype
leak:libharfbuzz

# Xlib / xcb display-side allocations held for the life of the connection.
leak:libX11
leak:libxcb
